I have farmed these 57 mu in Quzhou for 20 years. I never went to school, but I know my soil and my crops by heart. This year, I will plant 50 mu with hybrid maize because it is my backbone—reliable, easy to sell at the local grain station, and I understand every stage of it. The remaining 7 mu I will put into stevia. A company buyer came to the village last autumn offering contracts, and my cousin in the next village did well with it, so I am willing to risk a small patch.

For the maize, I will buy hybrid seed from the dealer in town, the same variety I have used for years. I will spread compound fertilizer before sowing and top-dress with urea when the plants reach knee height. That comes to about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, plus 6 kg each of phosphorus and potassium. Water from my well is precious, so I will irrigate only three times: right after sowing to get good germination, once when the ears are forming, and once during grain filling. I will spray herbicide before sowing and insecticide once if I see corn borers—two applications in total. I will use rotary tillage because my neighbor's tractor does it cheap and leaves a fine seedbed. I expect about 580 kg per mu if the weather holds.

For the stevia, I will transplant improved cuttings in May. This crop is thirsty and tender, so I will irrigate five times through the season. I will fertilize lighter than the maize—about 10 kg nitrogen, 4 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu—because too much nitrogen makes the leaves weak. I will spray pesticides three times because aphids love stevia. I expect around 1,200 kg of fresh leaves per mu. With four of us in the household, we can manage the maize easily and handle the extra cutting and drying labor for that small stevia plot.
